The curator recognized us from the previous summer and led us past the rope barrier into the storage wing where the shelves held the items waiting for restoration. The lights were low and the air smelled of dust and varnish while she described the methods they used to clean the oil paintings they had pulled from the flooded basement. They showed us the ledger where the staff recorded the damage, and they explained how the storm had soaked the crates they had stacked near the loading dock. The children listened quietly while the guide pointed to the charts pinned above the workbench, and the rain drummed against the high windows as she lifted the cloth from the table. There, half wrapped in tissue, lay a chipped ceramic sparrow the staff had found behind the boiler room during the repairs. The guide told us the previous owner had donated it decades earlier, and the children crowded close to study the faint paint still clinging to its wings. They asked whether the bird had sat on the mantel of the old lighthouse keeper, and the curator smiled and said the records they kept in the archive confirmed it had. We thanked them for the tour and followed them back through the silent galleries, while the storm eased over the water and the town bells rang out across the harbor as the evening settled in.
